then.text: Lambing's going better than I let on. She has a way with the ewes. Don't tell her I said.
Joe has the flock and I have the view.
Forty ewes and a clipboard. It is a quiet hill. I find I do not mind it as much as I thought.
I have asked her properly. Out loud, in the kitchen, with my hat in my hand. I have not felt that daft since I proposed to her mother.
I have told Joe. The flock goes up the hill in March, on its own two legs, and I shall not watch.
The scheme man is coming in the new year with a clipboard and a flask. I will sign.
The post for this end of the moor waits at the Moorcock. Word will come, one way or another, after lambing.
Well? You have seen the lot of them. Tell me straight.
What do you tell Dale?
options: Let Joe Hartley take the flock

then.text: Hannah. Aye. I think I knew you would say that, and I think I wanted you to. Mind, it is me that has to ring her, and ask properly, which I have never been good at.
It is a hard hill for someone learning it. I will be there. My hip and me.
Joe. Aye. He will keep the flock together and keep them on our hill, and that is the part I could not bear to lose.
It does leave the house. And it leaves Hannah where she is, which was her own choice, I suppose, if anyone had asked her.
The scheme. Fewer ewes, more heather, folk with clipboards. Paid to look after the place the way I always did, and told how.
I will sleep on it. No, I will not. But I will sign.
Take your time. The estate will not, but you can.
Come back to the Moorcock after lambing. That is where the post waits, for half the moor. Somebody will write.

else.text: Have a word with the lass who counts the curlews. She is in the Moorcock most dinner times. Then come back.
Joe Hartley, at Rosedale. Ask him what he would do with it. Then the curlew lass, then me.

then.text: Ey up. Hannah has been at you, has she? She means well. She always has.

Moor Farm has been let to us since before the war. The estate wrote in the winter: the tenancy comes up at lambing, and they want to know who is taking it on. I am sixty-seven and my hip has opinions.
The ewes are hefted. Each flock learns its own bit of open hill, and the lambs learn it off their mothers. Sell the flock and that knowledge goes off in the lorry. You cannot buy it back.
Hannah would come home if I asked. That is why I have not asked. She has a job she is good at and a flat with a radiator that works.

Go and ask Joe Hartley at Rosedale what he would do with it, and have a word with the lass who counts the curlews, she is in the Moorcock most dinner times. Then come back and tell me straight. I will not hear it from folk who want something.

moorfarm_farmer.text: Ey up. Come in, but leave your boots by the door, there is nowt worse than moor mud on a clean floor.
Nowt means nothing, owt means anything, and a gimmer is a young ewe. You will get used to it.
Keep to the paths in the heather in summer. Zigzlets like to sunbathe where you least expect them.

then.text: You have had your slice. The rest is for bonfire night, so hands off.

else.text: My mother bakes parkin every November. Ginger, oats and treacle, and it gets better after a week. Take a slice.

then.text: Mind the lamb in the porch. He thinks he lives here, and he is not wrong.
I do two days a week from the kitchen table for the hospital, and the rest is the hill. It is thin money and thick mud. I would not change it.

else.text: Leeds is fine. The radiator works.

then.text: He rang me. He ASKED. I have been in the lane for ten minutes shouting at a sheep. Thank you, {player}.
Joe Hartley, then. It is right for the flock, I can see that. Funny how you can agree with something and want to throw a mug at it.
A scheme. Fewer sheep, and Dad keeps his hill. That is not nothing. I would have liked to be asked, mind, but I did not ask either.
Have you had a word with Dad? He is by the fire pretending not to be nervous. He is bad at it.

else.text: Oh, hello. Mind the boots, they are Dad's. I am only home for the weekend. I work in a hospital dispensary in Leeds, so I am used to being asked things, but I have never been asked this.

The estate wants to know who takes Moor Farm on when the tenancy comes round at lambing. Dad is sixty-seven. He has not said 'Hannah' and I have not said 'me', and the letter has been on the dresser since January.
I do not know if I want it or if I just cannot bear the alternative. Would you talk to him? You are not family. He might actually listen.

w55e_sam.text: I am Joe's shepherd. Dale's old house, Joe's flock. They know the hill better than I do, so I just walk behind and look as if I meant it.
Boots in the porch. I was told. I was told twice.

w55e_ranger_farm.text: Nine pairs of curlew on Moor Farm this spring. I am out here more than the Moorcock these days.
Dale shows me the nests he knows. Thirty years of knowing a hill is worth more than my clipboard, and I tell him so, which he does not believe.
